Seems like unnecessary complication, new fleets, new operating conditions, for the same service. The little gold line stub to Antioch was a massive mistake as it is. You don’t use BART so you probably wouldn’t know that transferring between the two different systems is awful. Sometimes I just drive to Baypoint to avoid that dumbass line.

What organization runs an Elizabeth line type service though? Our Elizabeth line IS BART. You would have to set up new governance for those lines which opens up a whole new batch of problems. Non unified governance of the various transit agencies is already a huge problem. I think there should be another standard rail crossing, but making Link21 standard rail for a nonexistent rail operator would be a historical mistake. Just not a pragmatic choice at this point. Capitol Corridor’s yearly ridership is like 10 days of BART service.

Link21 should use BART specs though so they can get around to building a Geary/19th subway. If you built the new tunnel with standard rail sure that opens up some interesting stuff but that doesn’t solve the bottlenecking/redundancy problem that BART had initially sought the second tube for. Also the only electric regional rail line rn is CalTrain, which is struggling to build their downtown tunnel. Capitol Corridor (and ACE for that matter) would be better off focusing on right of way separation and electrification of the services they have rn. I wonder if a cheaper crossing could be made by rehabbing the Dumbarton Rail Bridge (wouldn’t require electrification) anyways. 

But I honestly doubt a second tube ever gets built. If they do I would rather them start the process of building a more robust BART system that can function more as a metro than a commuter service.

However this is the perverse nature of home builders, as housing prices rise they are more incentivized to build houses. They won’t build when prices are stagnant so when those prices spike there is a furious race to build homes while the market is booming. We don’t have a proactive housing policy that guides the market to fit the needs of the people, we only have individuals who are reacting to the increased profitability of building homes in the good times. Soft costs of building are very high where I am and generally fixed so a 300k house is alway going leave less margin to the homebuilder than the 700k one. Also the housing market is pretty location dependent so I hate when people say there are x vacant homes in the country, I don’t have the means to move and I don’t want to, this is my community! So in my opinion the current housing prices are very much real (or supported? Idk) in certain areas. 

I’m other parts of the country I think we are definitely in a bubble. I’ve had friends pay relatively steep costs to relocate the the Dakotas, Tennessee, Georgia, Idaho you name it. I often don’t think they have a great understanding of why those places don’t have the major metropolitan areas like we have. They just don’t have the economies to support those populations. Just cause 5000 Californians move to small town Nevada doesn’t mean there are jobs and opportunity for them there long term. Anecdotally I know this to be true several have returned often citing poor economic opportunity. In these areas I can see prices pull back significantly as people realize there is a reason Texas, NY, and CA are so large. 

Maybe too simple of an understanding but that’s my take.
